title: “Monks, desire and lust for the eye is a defilement of the mind. Desire and lust for the ear … for the nose … for…
content: “Monks, desire and lust for the eye is a defilement of the mind. Desire and lust for the ear … for the nose … for the tongue … for the body … for the mind is a defilement of the mind. When a monk has abandoned these defilements in regard to these six sense bases, his mind inclines to renunciation. Having been fully saturated with renunciation, his mind becomes wieldy and he directly knows the things to be fully known.”

title: “Monks, if anyone would develop these four foundations of mindfulness for just seven days, one of two fruits could be expected: either final knowledge here…
content: “Monks, if anyone would develop these four foundations of mindfulness for just seven days, one of two fruits could be expected: either final knowledge here and now, or if there remains a trace of clinging, the state of non-return. Monks, this is the one-way path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, for the realization of Nibbāna – namely, the Four Foundations of Mindfulness.”

title: “Suppose, Rādha, young boys or girls are playing with sandcastles. As long as their desire, lust, love, thirst, passion, and craving for those sandcastles are…
content: “Suppose, Rādha, young boys or girls are playing with sandcastles. As long as their desire, lust, love, thirst, passion, and craving for those sandcastles are not fully abandoned, they still cling to them, delight in them, treasure them, and are attached to them. But when their desire, lust, love, thirst, passion, and craving for those sandcastles are fully abandoned, then they smash them, scatter them, demolish them with their hands and feet and no longer play with them. So too, Rādha, you should smash, scatter, demolish form and not play with it, being intent on the destruction of craving for form. The destruction of craving, Rādha, is Nibbāna.”

title: “And, monks, shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, this body of the wise person is generated. That ignorance the wise person abandons. That craving…
content: “And, monks, shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, this body of the wise person is generated. That ignorance the wise person abandons. That craving the wise person destroys. Why is that? Monks, the wise person lives the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, with the breakup of the body, after death, the wise person does not go to another body. Not going to another body, he is freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is freed from suffering.”

title: “Furthermore, Sāriputta, a monk should reflect: ‘Have I abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure?’ Sāriputta, if a monk, on reflection, knows: ‘I have not…
content: “Furthermore, Sāriputta, a monk should reflect: ‘Have I abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure?’ Sāriputta, if a monk, on reflection, knows: ‘I have not yet abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure,’ then he should strive to abandon them. But if, on reflection, he knows: ‘I have abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure,’ then he should dwell with joy and gladness, training day and night in wholesome states.”

title: Thus he abides contemplating the body as a body internally; or he abides contemplating the body as a body externally; or he abides contemplating the…
content: Thus he abides contemplating the body as a body internally; or he abides contemplating the body as a body externally; or he abides contemplating the body as a body both internally and externally. Or he abides contemplating the nature of arising in the body; or he abides contemplating the nature of passing away in the body; or he abides contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in the body. ‘There is a body,’ he establishes mindfulness just enough for knowledge and mindfulness. And he abides independent, not clinging to anything in the world. Thus, monks, a monk abides contemplating the body as a body.”

title: “I do not see any other contact, monks, that so obsesses and occupies the mind of a man as the contact of a woman. The…
content: “I do not see any other contact, monks, that so obsesses and occupies the mind of a man as the contact of a woman. The contact of a woman, monks, obsesses and occupies the mind of a man.”

title: “Householder, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does not delight in…
content: “Householder, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does not delight in those forms, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them, not depending on them, consciousness arises without clinging to them. Householder, a monk without clinging attains complete Nibbāna … Householder, there are tastes … Householder, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in those phenomena, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — because he does not delight, does not praise, and dwells without lust, not depending on them, consciousness arises without clinging to them. Without clinging, householder, that monk attains Nibbāna. This, householder, is the cause, this is the reason why some beings here and now attain complete Nibbāna.”

title: “Householder, having known that sensual desire is a defilement of the mind, that noble disciple abandons sensual desire, the defilement of the mind; having known…
content: “Householder, having known that sensual desire is a defilement of the mind, that noble disciple abandons sensual desire, the defilement of the mind; having known that ill-will is a defilement of the mind, he abandons ill-will; having known that sloth and torpor are defilements of the mind, he abandons sloth and torpor; having known that restlessness and remorse are defilements of the mind, he abandons restlessness and remorse; having known that doubt is a defilement of the mind, he abandons doubt. This, householder, is called a noble disciple of great wisdom, of broad wisdom, who has entered the sphere of clear vision, endowed with wisdom. This is called being endowed with wisdom.”

title: “Monks, what is a course of practice that is pleasant in the present but yields painful results in the future? Monks, there are some ascetics…
content: “Monks, what is a course of practice that is pleasant in the present but yields painful results in the future? Monks, there are some ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine, such a view: ‘There is no fault in sensual pleasures.’ They indulge in sensual pleasures. Having indulged, at the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a plane of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell. There they experience painful, sharp, severe feelings. They say: ‘Those venerable ascetics and brahmins who see the future danger in sensual pleasures, who speak of the abandoning of sensual pleasures, who describe the full understanding of sensual pleasures—but we, with these sensual pleasures as the cause, as the condition, experience these painful, sharp, severe feelings.’ Monks, this is called a course of practice that is pleasant in the present but yields painful results in the future.”
